analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare drug benefit run by private insurers, with federal premium subsidies and a coverage gap.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 221-208 on June 28, 2002 — 212 of 223 Republicans for it, 199 of 208 Democrats against — but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a prescription drug benefit to Medicare for the first time, starting in 2005. The benefit would be delivered entirely through private insurance plans that receive large federal subsidies, with the government barred from negotiating drug prices directly. It also includes a gap in coverage where seniors pay full drug costs out of pocket, plus a long list of Medicare payment increases for hospitals, home health agencies, nursing homes, and doctors.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without drug coverage — especially low-income seniors, who would get full premium subsidies and $2-$5 copays. Also rural hospitals, home health agencies, skilled nursing facilities, hospices, and physicians, who receive payment increases. And the private insurers and drug plans that would permanently administer the new benefit under federal subsidy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors without drug coverage, plus providers and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit available to every Medicare beneficiary starting January 1, 2005, with a $250 deductible, 80% coverage on drug costs up to $1,000, and catastrophic coverage after $3,700 in out-of-pocket costs.
Gives people below 150% of the federal poverty line a full premium subsidy and low copays of $2 for generic drugs and $5 for other prescriptions, with a sliding-scale subsidy up to 175% of poverty.
Requires plans to accept all applicants regardless of health status and bars premium increases based on health for people who stay continuously covered.
Provides immediate help before the benefit starts: an endorsed prescription drug discount card program and assistance for low-income beneficiaries purchasing outpatient drugs.

Raises Medicare payments to rural hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, hospices, home health agencies (eliminating a scheduled 15% rate cut), and physicians, extends the moratorium on therapy caps, and adds coverage for a first preventive physical exam and cholesterol screening.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the premium subsidies to private plans, the low-income benefits, and the provider payment increases. Beneficiaries pay monthly premiums, a $250 deductible, and the full cost of drugs between $2,001 and $3,700 out of pocket. States are barred from imposing premium taxes on the new drug plans and from regulating them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, seniors in the coverage gap, and states

drawbacks.text: The benefit has a large gap: enrollees pay 100% of drug costs between $2,001 and $3,700 before catastrophic coverage begins, so seniors with expensive ongoing prescriptions would still face thousands of dollars in yearly bills.

The government would not negotiate drug prices. Instead, private plans negotiate, and the bill says prices negotiated by prescription drug plans may not be counted toward the Medicaid 'best price' calculation — removing a lever that currently pushes prices down.

The entire benefit is routed through private prescription drug plans and Medicare+Choice plans, which receive federal subsidies covering about two-thirds of their drug costs — locking private insurers in as the permanent channel for a public benefit.
Starting in 2005, seniors could no longer buy new Medigap policies that include drug coverage, pushing existing Medigap customers into the new private drug plans.

Federal standards would supersede state regulation of Medicare+Choice plans (except licensing and solvency rules), and states are prohibited from imposing premium taxes on the new drug plans — cutting states out of oversight.
The bill bundles substantial Medicare payment increases for hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and physicians, adding to federal costs beyond the drug benefit itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A Medicare drug benefit would have been a real gain for tens of millions of seniors who had none, and the low-income subsidies in this bill are genuinely generous. But the design matters as much as the benefit: money flows through private plans at a 67% federal subsidy, the government is barred from negotiating drug prices, and the middle of the benefit is a gap where sicker seniors pay full freight — so much of the new federal spending ends up as plan revenue rather than coverage. The provider payment increases are a further cost layered on. The bill gives seniors something they did not have, but on terms that permanently entrench the private insurance and pharmacy benefit management industries in the middle of the program.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 221-208 in June 2002, but the Senate simply placed it on its calendar and never voted; it died when the Congress ended in January 2003. A very similar private-plan design became law a year later in the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Nancy Johnson introduced the bill on June 18, 2002, and the Ways and Means Committee marked it up and reported it amended within eight days, on June 26.
The Rules Committee structured debate so the bill was closed to amendments, with only a motion to recommit allowed before the final vote.
On June 28, the Democratic motion to recommit — with instructions to add its terms — failed 204-223, with 203 of the House's 208 Democrats in favor and 220 of 223 Republicans opposed.
The bill then passed 221-208: 212 of 223 House Republicans voted yes, 199 of 208 Democrats voted no, and the two independents split.

The Senate received the bill on July 8, 2002, read it twice, and placed it on its legislative calendar under General Orders on July 15. No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, seniors gained nothing and lost nothing — they went without a drug benefit for another year and a half. The private-plan, no-negotiation architecture this bill set out was largely enacted the following year in the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003, so the longer-run beneficiaries were the private insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug manufacturers that became the permanent middlemen of Medicare's drug benefit, with coverage not reaching seniors until 2006.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers, via the 2003 law

for.name: Nancy L. Johnson
for.role: House sponsor; senior Republican on Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Ways and Means Committee markup, which reported it amended on June 26, 2002.

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor within ten days of introduction under a rule that closed it to amendments, allowing only a motion to recommit.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress to enact a Medicare drug benefit in 2002 and backed the House Republican approach.

against.name: 199 of 208 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, objecting to the private-plan design and the coverage gap.

against.name: Dick Gephardt
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to the committees, a procedural attempt to change the bill before the final vote; it failed 204-223.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House bill to a Senate vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar in July 2002.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Backed a competing drug benefit approach that relied less on private plans, which the Senate debated instead of the House bill.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split almost entirely on party lines: 212 of 223 House Republicans voted yes and 199 of 208 Democrats voted no; the motion to recommit failed 204-223 with 203 Democrats in favor and 220 Republicans opposed.

industries.industry: Private health insurers (Medicare+Choice organizations and prescription drug plan sponsors)
industries.note: The bill makes private plans the permanent, exclusive channel for Medicare's new drug benefit, paying them federal subsidies equal to about two-thirds of plan drug costs (37% direct plus 30% reinsurance). It also preempts state regulation of their plans and bars states from taxing their premiums. Their revenue stream depends on keeping a directly administered Medicare benefit and government price negotiation off the table.

The bill contains no government negotiation of drug prices; prices are negotiated only by private plans, and it explicitly excludes plan-negotiated prices from the Medicaid 'best price' calculation. Drug makers keep pricing leverage while gaining millions of newly insured customers.

Because the benefit is delivered through private plans rather than Medicare itself, PBMs' plan-side negotiating and administration role expands, and the bill directs a new Medicaid commission to consider promoting 'private enterprise models' including pharmacy benefit managers.

industries.industry: Health care providers (rural hospitals, home health agencies, skilled nursing facilities, hospices, physicians)
industries.note: The bill raises Medicare payment rates across the board: eliminating a scheduled 15% home health cut, raising the nursing component of skilled nursing payments, boosting rural and critical access hospital payments, and setting a 2% physician update. More revenue for providers generally means more service availability for seniors.

Starting in 2005 the bill bans new Medigap policies with drug coverage, closing off that product line, but guarantees existing Medigap drug customers a right to re-enter Medigap plans without health-based pricing if they switch to a private drug plan and back out.
